sentences.text: The hard problem here is sim-to-real transfer for a humanoid: a policy that scores well in MuJoCo often fails on hardware because of actuator latency, contact modeling errors and state estimation noise.
A common interface over thirteen policies is useful because each open-source policy usually ships with its own observation ordering, action scaling and PD gains, which makes comparisons unfair.

The approach looks ordinary as research, since benchmarking in simulation is a well-trodden method, but the C++ and ONNX focus points toward deployment-grade inference rather than Python research code.

A simulator-only waypoint tour does not measure the thing that matters most, which is whether the policy survives real hardware, so the benchmark's value depends on whether it is later tied to hardware results.

Low-cost humanoids such as the Unitree G1 have made walking research accessible, and a pool of open-source policies has built up that can be compared, which is what makes a thirteen-policy benchmark possible.
The repository was created on 2026-09-01, so this is a very recent effort that rides the open-source humanoid locomotion wave rather than leading it.
Teams buying or deploying humanoids need a neutral way to choose a controller, and a shared C++ interface lowers the cost of swapping policies on a real robot.
The likely buyers are humanoid integrators, robotics research labs and companies evaluating locomotion stacks, who would pay for validated, deployable controllers and evaluation tooling.
An open benchmark is normally given away, so revenue would have to come from something layered on top, such as a hosted evaluation service, certified policies or hardware-in-the-loop testing.
The evidence contains no customer, pricing or revenue information, so market size is not supportable from this record.

sentences.text: Technical risk: rankings in MuJoCo may not predict hardware performance, so the benchmark could reward policies that exploit simulator contact quirks and then fail on a real G1.
Commercial risk: the core asset is open source and benchmarks are rarely paid for, so the people who would use it, mostly researchers, are the least likely to pay.
Competition risk: Unitree or large simulation and robot-learning groups could publish an official evaluation suite and make a third-party benchmark redundant.
Team risk: with no named founders in the public record, we cannot judge whether anyone has the hardware deployment experience needed to move from a benchmark to a product.
The public record does not say who the founders are, whether rhoyn is a company or one person's project, or whether it has raised money.
It does not show whether any of the thirteen policies were tested on a physical G1, or how the scoring handles falls and recovery.
It does not show what the product is beyond the benchmark, or who has used the benchmark outside the three forks.
